newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian interior minister proposed as premier.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian interior minister proposed as premier.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists on Tuesday nominated powerful Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev as prime minister to head Bulgaria's ninth government since the end of one-party rule in 1989.
If his nomination is approved, Dobrev will form a new cabinet shortly to tackle the country's grave economic crisis.

A Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) spokeswoman said Dobrev's nomination had first to be approved by the Socialists' parliamentary allies and then voted on in parliament, where the ruling party has a majority.
The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) said on Tuesday it was stepping up anti-government protests to call for early parliamentary elections.
UDF leader Ivan Kostov told a news conference: "The BSP has proved that it has no potential to lead the country out of the crisis so we will take our responsibility to head the people's protest."
The UDF has scheduled street rallies in Sofia on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday.
Tens of thousands of protesters marched in Sofia last week and in two major cities on Monday to protest against shrinking wages eroded by the collapsing national currency.

If Dobrev, 49, is approved he will replace Zhan Videnov, who quit as premier and BSP leader at a party congress on December 21. Videnov's resignation, after months of criticism of his handling of the economy, sparked a showdown between hardliners and reformists.
"Dobrev was the only politician in the Socialist government who met the approval of all political forces," said Krassen Stanchev, director of the Institute for Market Economics.

Dobrev was responsible for human resources issues in the BSP for several years and became interior minister in May after his predecessor Lyubomir Nachev was dismissed for failing to deal with escalating crime.

Dobrev is perceived as one of the party's strongmen due to the great access to information provided by his posts, political analysts say. Bulgarian police files from the communist era have never been made public as they were in East Germany.
Stanchev said many deputies in parliament had business interests and would probably not welcome a figure who may crack down on any attempts to use public power for private interests.
"It is likely Dobrev will pass the vote by only a narrow margin, as many deputies have reasons to prefer a weaker figure for a prime minister," he added.
Parliament is expected to vote later this week.

Dobrev emerged as an outspoken critic of Videnov at the congress, where he attacked the cabinet's record in handling the country's economic crisis and raised the previously taboo issue of government corruption.
A mining engineer by training, Dobrev was a leader of the communist youth organisation Komsomol before 1989. He has also chaired parliament's national security committee.
Critics of his candidature say he lacks the economic expertise necessary to win the approval of Bulgaria's foreign partners.

International Monetary Fund officials have said that once a new government is formed they are prepared to complete talks on implementation of a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime proposed as a last resort to restore confidence in the crumbling financial system.

Two IMF missions visited Bulgaria in December to help the government and central bank prepare the introduction of a currency board, which is expected to halt the collapse of the national currency and curb inflation.

One of the first tasks of the new government may be to redraft the 1997 budget. Economists criticised the draft introduced to parliament by Videnov last week, saying its economic assumptions were unrealistic.
